claims.text: The exceptional ethanol-oxidation performance of the PGM nanoscale catalyst arises from a dynamically maintained, self-limiting surface oxide or subsurface oxygen layer.
The oxide or subsurface oxygen layer optimizes the adsorption energies of ethanol and its reaction intermediates.
The oxide or subsurface oxygen layer minimizes poisoning by strongly bound species such as CO.
The oxide or subsurface oxygen layer promotes complete 12-electron/12-proton oxidation of ethanol to CO2.
Pt or Pt-Ru alloy nanoparticles form a self-limiting surface or subsurface oxide layer under standard oxygenated operating conditions.
A mild reducing pretreatment or in situ reducing environment will remove or reduce subsurface oxygen.
Under normal conditions, the self-limiting oxide layer changes surface binding energies in a way that facilitates C-C bond cleavage.
The oxide layer facilitates full oxidation of ethanol to CO2.
The oxide layer prevents the accumulation of poisoning intermediates.
Reducing the catalyst's oxygen content alters adsorption properties so that partial oxidation pathways are favored.
Reducing the catalyst's oxygen content lowers catalyst durability.
Lowering surface oxygen will decrease overall ethanol-oxidation activity.
Lowering surface oxygen will shift the product distribution away from CO2 and toward acetaldehyde or acetate.
Lowering surface oxygen will reduce durability because poisoning becomes more severe.
Under standard oxygenated conditions, the oxide layer is naturally maintained and produces high activity, selectivity, and durability.
The proposed mechanism applies to liquid-phase ethanol oxidation over nanoscale PGM catalysts at moderate temperatures.
The proposed mechanism may fail under high-temperature gas-phase conditions or on surfaces with substantially different oxide dynamics.
The precise structure, composition, and operating-state dynamics of the proposed subsurface oxide are not fully characterized.
The hypothesis would be rejected if reducing surface or subsurface oxygen fails to decrease activity, shift products toward partial oxidation, or change durability relative to the oxygenated control.
